def: abstinent or austere in lifestyle (adj); a person who leads an austere and simple life without material pleasures, esp. someone who does this for religious reasons

def: Reach the highest point or final stage

def: Burdensome, oppressive, hard to endure

def: Ordinary, dull, commonplace

example: During the Gold Rush, speculators bought up land, sometimes with borrowed funds, expecting to prospect the land for gold and get rich quickly.

def: Occasional, happening irregularly or in scattered locations
example: Her attendance was sporadic at best, so when she flounced into class after a two-session absence, she discovered that not only was everyone working on group projects, but that the professor hadn’t even thought to assign her to a group.

def: Playful, merry, joking around, done “in sport” (rather than intended seriously)
example: After Will shot a ball entirely off the pool table, knocking a woman’s purse off a bar stool, his friends laughed hysterically and called him “purse-snatcher” all night, but he took it as sportive and bought the next round of drinks.

def: Status, rank, reputation (noun); existing indefinitely, not movable (adj)
example: As he had feared, his divorce greatly reduced his standing as a relationship expert.

def: Complete, total, utter; harsh or grim; extremely simple, severe, blunt, or plain
example: The designer’s work is appreciated for its stark beauty, but most people prefer to live in a cozier, more welcoming home—the kind with carpets and pillows, for instance.

def: Fixed, not moving or changing, lacking vitality
example: The anthropologist studied a society in the Amazon that had been deliberately static for hundreds of years—the fiercely proud people disdained change, and viewed all new ideas as inferior to the way of life they had always practiced.

def: Existing state or condition
example: Many opposed the establishment of a needle-exchange program, but others reasoned that the plan would be an improvement on the status quo, in which disease spread rapidly through certain communities.

def: Not generous with money, reluctant to spend or give
example: Billionaire industrialist J. Paul Getty was so famously stingy that he installed pay phones in his mansion for guests to use. When his grandson was kidnapped, he refused to pay ransom and only changed his mind when the kidnappers cut off the boy’s ear. This famous cheapskate then demanded that his son (the boy’s father) pay him back! What a miser.

def: Indifferent to pleasure or pain, enduring without complaint; person indifferent to pleasure or pain (noun)
example: Della was not only calm but positively stoic, thanking her family for driving her home from chemotherapy, and then simply never mentioning it until it was time to go again.

def: Unemotional, showing little emotion, not easily moved
example: Dad is so stolid that we can’t get a rise out of him no matter what we do—Jody got a tattoo, Max declared himself a communist, and Helen won a Rhodes Scholarship. No response! Dad just nods and says “Alright, then.”

def: Block, hinder, or thwart (verb); an obstacle (noun)
example: Sara feared that her learning disability would stymie her success in college, but the support services offered were excellent and she was fine academically; the thing that really stymied her college career was poor time management.

def: Existing in the mind or relating to one’s own thoughts, opinions, emotions, etc.; personal, individual, based on feelings
example: Naturally, anyone’s experience of a movie is subjective, and some will enjoy this picture despite its flaws; however, it is an objective fact that the cinematography is very bad.

def: Sink, settle down, become less active; return to a normal level
example: When her terror subsided, she realized that the house wasn’t really haunted.

def: Support with evidence or proof; give a material existence to
example: You say you were at home when the crime occurred two towns over—is there anyone who can substantiate your claim?

def: Coming after or following
example: After the sale of the company, you will receive 5% of the profits from the current year, and 1% in all succeeding years.

def: Replace, take the position of, cause to be disregarded as void or obsolete
example: Of course, electric washing machines superseded hand-powered ones many decades ago, but my great-grandmother used her hand-cranked washer until she died in the 1990s.

def: Pray humbly; ask, beg, or seek in a humble way
example: She had been estranged from her wealthy father for years, but when she needed money for her daughter’s medical care, she supplicated the old man for assistance.

def: Excess, excessive amount, overindulgence
example: The soup kitchen would like to announce that it has a serious surfeit of those cans of jellied cranberries that no one seems to want, but it could still use at least ten Thanksgiving turkeys.

def: Guess, infer, think or make an opinion with incomplete information
example: Based on your rather sad attempt to figure out the tip on our restaurant bill, I would surmise that you actually have no idea how percents work.

def: Servile flatterer, parasitic person who fawns in order to get ahead
example: Stop being such a sycophant. I don’t need you to compliment my tie or get me coffee; I just need you to do your job without bothering me.

def: Happening at the same time; occurring at the same rate and thus happening together repeatedly
example: The sound of that bell is a signal for the dancers to make perfectly synchronous entrances from opposite sides of the stage.

def: Lay aside to discuss later, often as a way to postpone discussion indefinitely
example: I see we’re not going to agree on whether to scrap our entire curriculum and develop a new one, so let’s table that discussion and move on to voting on the budget.

def: Understood without being said; implied, not stated directly; silent
example: Her parents never told her she could smoke, but they gave their tacit consent when they didn’t say anything about the obvious smell coming from her bedroom.

def: Not talking much, reserved; silent, holding back in conversation
example: Because he felt self-conscious about his stutter, Mike had always been taciturn, but after some very good speech therapy, soon he was much more voluble.

def: Only slightly relevant, going off-topic
example: It’s hard to get a quick answer out of Noah—ask him any question, and you’ll get a wide range of tangential remarks before you can find a polite way to move on.

def: Moderation, self-control, esp. regarding alcohol or other desires or pleasures; total abstinence from alcohol
example: After the end of the Civil War, economic change led to an increase in alcohol problems and the birth of the Temperance Movement, which ultimately led to Prohibition.

def: Long and thin, slender; flimsy, having little substance
example: Your argument is quite tenuous—it depends on our accepting the results of a 1955 study published in an obscure medical journal not subject to peer review.

def: Well-timed, happening at a suitable time
example: Your arrival is quite timely—we were just mulling over a question we’re sure you can answer!

def: Fearful, timid
example: An expression describing a timorous person is “quaking in his boots”—that is, a scared person would shake or shiver from fear.

def: Bitter, abusive criticism or verbal attack
example: I hate that television show where that commentator goes on angry tirades about all the liberal conspiracies taking over America. Even my conservative friends find his ranting embarrassing.

def: Sluggishness, lethargy, or apathy; a period of inactivity
example: Sam had hoped to be able to play in the game after having his wisdom teeth out, but the anesthesia left him in such torpor that he obviously couldn’t play soccer.

def: Very hot, parching, burning; passionate
example: They had a torrid love affair in the ‘80s, but split up because a royal was not permitted to marry a commoner.

def: Easily controlled or managed, docile; easily shaped or molded
example: He’s a tractable fellow—when I asked if we could see a different movie than the one we’d come to see, he shrugged and said “Cool.”

def: Temporary, short-lived, not lasting
example: While a few people marry their high school sweethearts, generally, our teenage years are full of transitory crushes.

def: Trivial, not very important; so small as to be unimportant; frivolous, shallow
example: Luis broke up with Cara because she was always obsessed with some trifling matter—he tried to talk about foreign aid dependency, and she changed the subject to what the actress Katie Holmes dressed her daughter Suri in for a shopping trip.

def: Lacking freshness and originality, lacking effectiveness due to overuse, cliché
example: The topic of your speech is “Children are the Future”? That’s pretty trite. Maybe you should think harder and come up with something original.

def: Existing everywhere at the same time
example: Thirty years ago, women would lie about coloring their hair, considering the admission embarrassing. Today, blatantly fake hair color—not to mention fake tans and unnaturally white teeth— are ubiquitous, not only on starlets, but even on the checkers at the local grocery store.

def: Weaken, cause to collapse by digging away at the foundation (of a building or an argument); injure or attack in a secretive or underhanded way
example: Rather than searching impartially for the truth, these pharmaceutical company “scientists” willfully ignored any evidence that undermined the conclusion they were being paid to produce.

def: Emphasize (or, literally, to underline text)
example: “You’re not going to mess with Joey anymore,” said Joey. His new bodyguards stepped forward threatening, as though to underscore Joey’s point.

def: Dig up, uncover, expose
example: The ACLU’s Prison Project works tirelessly to unearth evidence from old cases that might exonerate innocent people who have spent years or even decades in prison.

def: Unambiguous, clear, absolute; having only one possible meaning
example: Although Chuck denied he had a problem, his family was unequivocal in demanding that he check into rehab. Chuck knew there was no getting around it this time.

def: Never before known or seen, without having happened previously
example: When Nixon resigned, American bravado was at an all-time low—the resignation of a sitting President was disgraceful and unprecedented.

def: Improper, inappropriate, against the rules of taste or politeness
example: The activist really did want to get the candidate’s support for the equal-rights measure, so she did what the candidate’s aides asked—but she found it very unseemly that they suggested a specific dollar amount for the “donation” she was asked to make in order to get a meeting.

def: Waver in one’s mind or opinions, be indecisive
example: In need of a good used car, I was vacillating between the Ford and the Hyundai until a recommendation from a friend helped me decide.

def: Revere, regard with deep respect and awe
example: The boys were utterly crushed when the baseball player they venerated saw them waiting and refused to sign an autograph.

def: Truthfulness, accuracy; habitual adherence to the truth
example: I question the veracity of your story—I just don’t think you’ve been to outer space.

def: Wordy
example: Twitter’s 140 character limit really forces the verbose to go against their natural tendencies and instead write succinctly.

def: Capable of living (or growing, developing, etc.); practical, workable
example: I have three screenplay ideas, but the studio head said only one was commercially viable. Apparently, it’s important to have a human lead character and a satisfying ending.

def: Related to items of high quality from a previous era, old-fashioned, antique (adj); the wine of a particular year (noun)
example: He didn’t want just any vintage Darth Vader action figure—he wanted a particular vintage, the 1978 telescoping lightsaber one.

def: Existing only in the mind or by means of a computer network; existing in results or in essence but not officially or in name
example: The Tamagotchi is a handheld virtual pet made in Japan—you have to “care” for it by performing various actions with the device, but in the end, your “pet” still looks very much like a keychain.

def: Verbally abuse, rebuke or criticize harshly
example: All couples fight, but your girlfriend vituperates you so severely that I’m not sure she loves you at all. Verbal abuse is actually a pretty good reason to break up.

def: Varying, inconstant, fleeting; tending to violence, explosive;
example: Following the sudden revolution, the political environment in the country was so volatile that anything could have started a riot.

def: Justified, authorized (warrant can mean to justify or a justification, but can also mean to vouch for or guarantee)
example: The pundit’s comments don’t even warrant a response from our organization—they were mere name-calling, not suitable for public discourse.

def: Watchful, motivated by caution, on guard against danger
example: Be wary of anyone who tells you that “anyone” can get rich with some special plan or scheme.

def: While on the contrary, considering that
example: Mr. Katsoulas had always assumed his son would take over the family business, whereas his son had always assumed he would go away to college and never come back.

def: Marked or motivated by whims (odd, fanciful ideas); erratic, unpredictable
example: Alice in Wonderland is a famously whimsical story in which a little girl falls down a rabbit hole and finds a strange and at times absurd world.

def: Crafty, cunning, characterized by tricks or artifice
example: The wily criminal stole eight laptops by simply walking into a branch of a large company, introducing himself as the laptop repairman, and waiting for people to hand him their computers.

def: Great fervor or enthusiasm for a cause, person, etc., tireless diligence in furthering that cause; passion, ardor
example: Whether you agree with their views or not, you have to admit that the employees of PETA have great zeal for animal rights—most work for less than $25,000 a year, and often participate in protests that get them shouted at or even arrested.

def: High point, culmination
example: At the zenith of her career, the actress could command $5 million per film. Now, she is mostly seen in made-for-TV movies.
